title: Maintain and conserve the flora in nature areas

lessons.title: Indigenous flora and the threats to it
lessons.html:
Indigenous flora and the threats to it

Flora means the plants of an area. Nature areas include nature reserves, conservancies, wetlands, river banks, natural veld on farms and estates, and natural parts of parks and golf courses. South Africa has one of the richest floras in the world. The Cape fynbos alone has thousands of plant types found nowhere else. Grasslands, savanna, Karoo, forest and wetlands each have their own special plants.

Why plants in nature areas matter

  • They hold the soil and stop erosion.
  • They keep rivers and wetlands healthy and clean water.
  • They feed and shelter animals, birds and insects, including bees that pollinate crops.
  • They give grazing, medicine, thatch and beauty, and support tourism jobs.

Threats

ThreatEffect
Invasive alien plants (for example wattles, pines, lantana, bugweed, prickly pear)Spread fast, crowd out indigenous plants, use a lot of water, increase fire risk
Overgrazing and tramplingBare soil, erosion, loss of good grasses
Wrong fire regimeToo frequent, too hot or no fire at all can all harm veld types
ErosionTopsoil and plants washed away, dongas form
Illegal plant collectingRare plants such as cycads and succulents removed
Pollution and dumpingPoisons soil and water

The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 deals with the control of weeds and invader plants and with protecting soil and veld. Many indigenous plants are also protected by national and provincial laws. Never remove or damage protected plants without a permit. If you are not sure whether a plant is protected, ask.

lessons.title: Conservation tasks in the field
lessons.html:
Conservation tasks in the field

Clearing invasive alien plants

  • Learn to recognise the main invaders in your area. Your supervisor will show you.
  • Pull up small seedlings by hand, roots and all, when the soil is moist.
  • Larger plants are cut and the stump treated with an approved herbicide by trained workers, following the label. Some regrow if only cut.
  • Do follow-up visits. New seedlings come up from seeds in the soil for years.
  • Do not spread seeds: clean boots, clothes and tools before moving to a clean area.
  • Work from the least invaded areas towards the worst, so cleared areas stay clean.

Controlling erosion

  • Pack brush (cut branches) or stones across small gullies to slow water.
  • Build small stone or log barriers across paths that channel water.
  • Replant bare areas with indigenous grasses or plants as instructed.
  • Keep vehicles on roads and people on paths.

Caring for indigenous plants

  • Do not damage plants when working; walk carefully and keep to paths.
  • Collect seed or cuttings only as instructed and with permission.
  • Plant indigenous plants in the right place and season, and water them until established.
  • Report rare or unusual plants to your supervisor.

Recording

Write down what you did, where, and how much: hectares cleared, number of plants planted, erosion structures built. Photos before and after are useful. Records show progress and help plan follow-up.

Safety

  • Wear boots, gloves, long sleeves, a hat and eye protection.
  • Only trained and authorised workers use chainsaws, brush cutters and herbicides.
  • Watch for snakes, bees and ticks.
  • Stop work during lightning.
  • Carry water and a first aid kit, and never work alone.

Key points

  • South Africa's indigenous flora is rich and valuable.
  • Invasive alien plants, overgrazing, erosion and wrong fire regimes are the main threats.
  • Clear invaders properly and do follow-up visits.
  • Slow water and replant to control erosion.
  • Protected plants may not be removed without a permit; record all work done.
